en: When ice absorbs heat from its surroundings, its water molecules gain energy and vibrate faster until they break their rigid structure to become liquid water.
Heating liquid water gives its molecules enough kinetic energy to overcome intermolecular forces, allowing them to escape into the air as invisible water vapor.
When warm water vapor touches a cold glass, the gas molecules lose thermal energy, slow down, and clump together to form liquid water droplets.
Stirring sugar in water breaks the solid sugar crystals into individual molecules that spread evenly between water molecules, creating a uniform sweet solution.
Exposing iron to oxygen and moisture triggers a chemical reaction that rearranges the atoms to form a brittle, reddish-brown solid called iron oxide.
Burning wood combines its carbon compounds with oxygen in the air, releasing heat and light while transforming the solid into ash and carbon dioxide gas.
Cooling liquid water below zero degrees Celsius removes kinetic energy from its molecules, causing them to lock into a fixed, hexagonal crystalline structure as ice.
Pouring a sand-water mixture through filter paper traps the solid sand particles in the pores while allowing the liquid water to flow through into the container.
Bringing a magnet near iron filings exerts a magnetic force that pulls the metallic particles toward the magnet, separating them from non-magnetic sand.
Because wood has a lower density than water, the upward buoyant force of the displaced water pushes the wooden block to float on the surface.
Heating a metal bridge causes its atoms to vibrate more vigorously and push apart, making the solid metal expand and lengthen on hot days.
Shaking oil and vinegar temporarily breaks the oil into tiny droplets that disperse through the vinegar, but they quickly separate again due to differing densities.
